extracted.intended_audience: emerging photographers and aspiring/early-career photo editors at editorial publications
extracted.subtask_description: Practical career and craft guidance for photographers who want to work as editorial photo editors — covering editing & sequencing practice, hiring/assignment criteria, producing visual-first stories, portfolio-building, and community/access strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing and sequencing are essential to visualizing a story
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing and sequencing are integral to shaping narrative and visualizing a story; an editor's choices create meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pairing, juxtaposition, surprise and tension to build narrative. Example: creating narratives by pairing contrasting or echoing images; editing produces narrative when context is removed (books/sequence) vs. collaborating with text (online/print).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use movement, color, and shape as guiding principles in sequencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Movement, color, and shape should guide how images are ordered so that a sequence flows and resonates visually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how visual elements lead the viewer through a sequence; these principles help create coherence and emotional rhythm when sequencing photos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairing images to create surprise, tension, and echo
rubrics_metrics.description: Create surprise and tension by pairing contrasting or echoing images together to generate new meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: juxtaposing disparate images (e.g., Joshua tree with a black-and-white arm reaching) to mirror themes and create symbolism across different times/places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-specific editing: adapt approach to format
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing differs by medium: editing for a book or standalone sequence (where context is removed) is different from editing for an online story or print spread that must work with text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For books/sequences the edit creates the narrative; for online/print you should work within and elevate the accompanying text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism and thematic motifs in editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use symbolic imagery and recurring motifs to build thematic layering and deeper interpretation within a body of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: using Joshua tree symbolism and astrological references (Gemini) within a series to signify themes like hope, duality, and flux.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hire photographers who can shoot like personal work
rubrics_metrics.description: When assigning photographers, prefer those who can shoot as if they are shooting personal work — both stylistically and contextually — so the images carry voice and impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerging photographers may lack large editorial portfolios but can bring a distinct voice; give them space for creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize diversity and range of voices in assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: As gatekeepers, editors should assign a range of voices and be deliberate about diversity and equity in who tells stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diversity is critical not only to cover one's own community but to apply diverse perspectives across reporting and features; The Times has influence to elevate emerging photographers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and logistical considerations in production (pandemic-era)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize photographer safety and adapt assignments based on access and safety constraints (e.g., shifting toward outdoor, environmental portraits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During restricted access, plan shoots that keep talent safe; expect some pandemic-era workflow changes not to persist but to adapt for safety when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Career-building tactics: portfolio reviews, outreach, and submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use portfolio reviews, email outreach to editors, submitting to platforms, and researching publications as primary strategies to get work seen by gatekeepers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Times runs free yearly portfolio reviews; social media is useful for exposure but follower count does not equal quality or success. Apply to open calls, online platforms, and use community resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internships, fellowships, and freelance experience as entry paths
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply for paid internships/fellowships or start freelancing as an editor to gain practical experience and access editorial opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal connections can help but are not the only route; recommended to seek paid/fellowship openings and freelance editing roles to build credentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start or get involved in online communities/publications to make connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Become active in online photo communities, email people you admire, or start your own publication to build a network and visibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from Celii's past: creating The Rotating Gallery, Fjord Photo, and collaborating with Humble Arts Foundation as ways to curate and showcase work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing practice technique: cut up contact sheets (tactile editing)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Cutting up your contact sheets like playing cards" — editing physically can change your seeing and editing decisions in ways digital-only workflows don't.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Working with tangible photos helps shift perspective away from screen-clicking and can reveal different sequencing options; recommended as a vital tool for editing and sequencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep making work and persist through rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejection is part of the process; continue producing new work and submitting despite setbacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: don't be dissuaded by rejection — apply broadly and maintain creative output (e.g., 100 days projects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend artistic practice with documentary/photojournalism skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine an artistic lens with documentary reporting and production skills to expand project possibilities and storytelling depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Celia plans projects that merge personal narrative and documentary reporting; producing visual-first stories often requires reporting and producing expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch and produce visual-first stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Concept and pitch visual-first story ideas; editors should be able to pitch visual concepts and enlist reporters/editors to execute them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an editor, grow from photo research tasks to pitching visual-first stories and coordinating reporters and editors to bring projects to life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of platform/technology's influence on photography exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: The Internet democratizes exposure but platform design affects whose work is seen; be aware of changing social platforms and the need for photo-first community tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social platforms (Instagram/TikTok shifts) can commodify community; there's a need for photo-first, community-oriented apps that don't restrict which work is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching and providing constructive criticism is a core editorial skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Being able to teach and give constructive criticism is an important part of the editor's role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience as a TA and organizing exhibitions informed Celii's ability to critique and mentor photographers; mentoring can help emerging photographers improve and access opportunities.
